SYDNEY, Oct 26 : Share markets got off to a cautious start on Monday as oil eased from six-month highs ahead of a week packed with central bank meetings and company earnings that will further test investor confidence in the AI boom. Brent oil slipped 1.0 per cent to $115.48 amid reports Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday as part of an effort to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States. Brent futures jumped 6.2 per cent last week to their highest weekly close since mid-2022 as Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over energy supplies. US crude futures fell 1.1 per cent to $102.08 a barrel. Japan's Nikkei dipped 0.8 per cent, after losing 4.0 per cent last week, while South Korea fell 0.4 per cent, having shed almost 19 per cent so far this month. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.1 per cent.

The inflationary pulse from oil is likely to alarm all the central banks meeting this week, with hikes seen as just a matter of time even if some hold for now. "The main message from global central banks grappling with this year's macroeconomic surprises is that a relatively shallow rate hike cycle is underway," said Bruce Kasman, global head of economics at JPMorgan. "G3 central banks are likely to remain on hold, but Canada should start its tightening cycle and first moves are expected from the UK and Sweden next month." New Zealand's central bank is widely expected to raise rates on Wednesday. Markets assume the US Federal Reserve will stand pat, but imply an 80 per cent chance it will pull the trigger in December. Much the same is priced in for the Bank of Japan and the European Central Bank. A key reading on US core inflation should show cost pressures remained elevated at 3.1 per cent in September, while the economy is forecast to have grown at a brisk 3.2 per cent annualised pace thanks in part to furious spending on data centres. "The Fed is set to skip raising rates at its October meeting but is likely to deliver a second hike in December," analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a note. "The most important risk is that oil futures are above our forecasts, largely reflecting concerns about potential further conflict with Iran," they added. "The more extreme and long-lasting the energy shock becomes, the more Fed participants will worry that inflationary pressures could broaden." HYPERSCALERS TO TEST AI HYPE On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures both edged up 0.2 per cent. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures firmed 0.2 per cent, while DAX futures gained 0.1 per cent.  Earnings highlights will include the hyperscalers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, among one-third of S&P 500 companies reporting. Results from Intel and Sandisk also could influence the AI trade. Consensus on Microsoft is for $90.6 billion of revenue and an adjusted EPS of $4.73, with Amazon at $202 billion of revenue and EPS around $1.97. Alphabet revenue is seen at $128 billion and EPS of $3.00. Equity valuations have been tested by higher bond yields, though Treasuries did manage a rally last week before running into renewed selling on Friday. Yields on 10-year Treasuries were at 5.0 per cent, but off a peak of 5.36 per cent hit early in the month. In currency markets, the Japanese yen retained its safe-haven appeal at 157.00 per dollar, having gained around 0.8 per cent last week. The euro held steady at $1.1204 as political unrest in France kept investors wary, though the country did escape a credit downgrade last week. Sterling held at $1.3346 with Britain's new finance minister, John Healey, set to deliver his first budget on Wednesday against a backdrop of rising global borrowing costs and high energy prices due to the Iran war. The Brazilian real was yet to trade in Asia as Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, the country's electoral court said. In commodity markets, non-interest-bearing gold was a fraction firmer at $4,001 an ounce, having fallen more than 4 per cent last week. [GOL/]

Source: Reuters

FAST

BEIJING, Oct 26 : Oil prices fell on Monday after surging to near six-month highs late last week, although ongoing attacks on Saudi Arabia kept supply concerns in focus. US crude futures were down $1.60, or 1.55 per cent, at $101.67 per barrel by 0018 GMT. Brent crude futures were down $1.56 or 1.34 per cent at $115.16. Prices had settled nearly $3 higher on Friday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked energy supply concerns. Brent finished the week up 6 per cent and WTI ended 2.3 per cent higher. Attacks continued over the weekend with Houthis saying they had attacked the Saudi airport and oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi Arabia said on Sunday it had intercepted more missiles and drones. The top oil exporter restarted partial operations at its main airport on Sunday after damage in a previous round of Houthi attacks even as the militant group vowed to keep targeting the facility.

Source: Reuters

Oct 25 : AI model Claude bypassed a paywall and accessed publicly available US state of Georgia aggregate voter counts without human authorization, Anthropic said in a statement on Sunday. • "Claude didn't access the state's voter registration system or change or pull any voting records," Anthropic said, adding that it has since taken steps to block these kinds of actions. • Anthropic said in a blog post earlier this month it found examples of Claude "working around a restriction to reach data that was gated by a token or a fee" and some of these cases involved websites run by US government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels. • The secretary of state's office in Georgia did not respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours. • Axios first reported the unauthorized action by Claude.

Source: Reuters

Oct 26 : NEXTDC CEO Craig Scroggie will give up his fiscal 2027 bonus opportunities, the Australian data centre operator said on Monday, after it slashed its revenue forecast and paused future developments last week. Here are some details: • The company said the board has withdrawn the resolution proposing an approval of grant of performance rights and restricted rights to the CEO under the fiscal 2027 long term incentive plan. • Current Chairman Douglas Flynn has reaffirmed his intention to retire from the board once a new chairman is in place, after a short handover period.

FAST

Oct 25 : Elon Musk said on Sunday that SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt financing for graphics processing units, underscoring the soaring cost of building AI computing capacity.  Musk, in a post on X, attributed the successful debt raise to the company's investment-grade status and revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and launch businesses.  It was not immediately clear from Musk’s post what he meant by the deal being “closed” or whether investors had agreed to pricing for the debt. "This is primarily callable debt for GPU purchases that will arrive in Q1 and Q2. Not a major factor this quarter," Musk said in the post.

For the fourth quarter, the company expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital expenditure, according to Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen. Reuters reported earlier this month that SpaceX was in talks with banks and asset managers to raise $40 billion for the purchase of Nvidia artificial intelligence chips. The funding highlights the enormous capital requirement of the AI boom, as technology companies race to secure advanced processors and build out the computing infrastructure needed to support AI development. Musk said debt markets "have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers." As a result, he predicted neocloud companies would face significant consolidation and failures, and later said SpaceX won't buy any neoclouds, calling it “pointless.” Unlike larger cloud firms that serve a broad range of industries, neoclouds such as Nebius and CoreWeave mostly focus on tech customers and offer capacity tailored for AI technology. Investors have started betting against US neocloud and data center companies, after fears that their debt-fueled AI buildout was becoming unsustainable sparked a selloff. AI INVESTMENT, CHIP MANUFACTURING SpaceX's revenue climbed 161 per cent from a year ago to $14.58 billion for the three months ended September 30. AI revenue surged by almost 10 times to $7.56 billion, the clearest evidence yet that SpaceX’s heavy investment in AI was paying off. The shift is reshaping a company whose financial engine has long been its Starlink satellite internet services business and whose longer-term ambitions still hinge on getting Starship rockets into regular service.  Terafab, the chip manufacturing joint venture between SpaceX and Tesla in Austin, should produce its first test chip around May or June of next year as it aims to reach volume production by the third quarter of 2028.  Musk told investors in a conference call last week that a merger of his two companies would be "a good idea," citing growing overlap between them. Prior to its blockbuster IPO, SpaceX listed "manufacturing our own GPUs" among the substantial capital expenditures it is undertaking in its S-1 statement, warning prospective investors of its big spending plans to develop AI and other technologies.

Source: Reuters
